name: Familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection
aliases: familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection

reference.source: ACC/AHA thoracic aortic disease guidance / clinical genetics references
clinicalPearls: Non-syndromic heritable predisposition to thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection, typically inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with variable penetrance
Pathogenic variants often involve genes of the smooth-muscle contractile apparatus (ACTA2, MYH11) and the transforming growth factor beta pathway (TGFBR1, TGFBR2)
Dissection can occur at smaller aortic diameters than in sporadic disease, so gene-specific thresholds guide intervention
A family history of aortic aneurysm, dissection, or unexplained sudden death is a key clue
First-degree relatives warrant screening imaging and genetic counselling
Management centres on blood pressure control with beta-blockade and/or angiotensin receptor blockade plus regular aortic surveillance
Elective repair is undertaken at gene- and family-specific size thresholds to pre-empt dissection
reference.pathophysiology: Familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection results from inherited defects that impair the integrity of the aortic wall. Variants in smooth-muscle contractile proteins such as ACTA2 and MYH11 weaken the ability of medial smooth-muscle cells to withstand haemodynamic stress, while variants affecting the transforming growth factor beta signalling pathway disturb extracellular matrix homeostasis. The resulting medial degeneration and loss of structural resilience predispose the thoracic aorta to progressive dilatation and to dissection, sometimes at diameters that would be considered low-risk in sporadic disease.
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography and CT or MR angiography of the thoracic aorta
Genetic testing with an aortopathy gene panel
Genetic counselling and cascade screening of first-degree relatives
Assessment for syndromic features of Marfan or Loeys-Dietz syndrome
Serial aortic imaging to track growth
Blood pressure assessment and cardiovascular risk evaluation
redFlags: Acute severe chest or back pain suggesting aortic dissection
Rapid increase in aortic diameter on surveillance
Family history of dissection or sudden death at small aortic size
Signs of aortic regurgitation or malperfusion
reference.prognosis: With genetic identification, family screening, blood pressure control, and timely prophylactic surgery at gene-specific thresholds, the risk of fatal dissection can be substantially reduced. Prognosis depends on the specific gene involved, some of which confer particularly aggressive disease.
pitfalls: Applying standard sporadic aneurysm size thresholds to genes that dissect at smaller diameters
Failing to screen and counsel first-degree relatives
Overlooking syndromic aortopathies such as Marfan or Loeys-Dietz syndrome
Neglecting long-term surveillance after initial normal imaging
references: ACC/AHA guideline for the diagnosis and management of aortic disease
Clinical genetics literature on heritable thoracic aortic disease
management: Lower aortic wall stress pharmacologically with beta-blockade and/or angiotensin receptor blockade to slow dilatation and reduce dissection risk
Undertake serial aortic imaging with echocardiography and CT or MR angiography at gene-specific intervals to track aneurysm growth
Offer prophylactic surgical repair of the thoracic aorta at gene-specific diameter thresholds, which are lower than in sporadic disease
Advise avoidance of heavy isometric or competitive exertion and sympathomimetic stimulants that provoke blood-pressure surges
Refer to a specialist aortopathy and cardiothoracic multidisciplinary team, with assessment for syndromic features of Marfan or Loeys-Dietz syndrome
Provide genetic counselling with cascade screening imaging and aortopathy gene-panel testing of first-degree relatives
Manage acute dissection as an emergency with anti-impulse therapy and urgent surgical assessment, escalating immediately for sudden severe chest or back pain
